The query “who had the right to vote” is broad and allows multiple valid perspectives across time. The documents provide complementary information about different groups (white male property owners, free Black men, women) and different periods (1776, 1787, 1870, 1920, etc.), without contradicting each other. Together they yield a comprehensive answer.

Originally, voting rights in the United States were determined by states and typically restricted to white male property owners [d2,d3,d5,d7,d9,d10]. Over time, amendments expanded the franchise: the 15th Amendment (1870) prohibited denial based on race, extending voting rights to African American men [d2,d3,d6,d7,d9], and the 19th Amendment (1920) granted women the right to vote nationwide [d2,d3,d4,d9]. Some states like New Jersey briefly allowed property-owning women and free Black men to vote earlier [d5,d8]. Today, citizens over age 18 cannot be denied the right to vote on the basis of race, religion, sex, disability, or sexual orientation [d9].
